question: A 9-year-old girl is diagnosed with Turner syndrome (45,X karyotype). She is currently at the 3rd centile for height with no signs of puberty. She has a bicuspid aortic valve (no current haemodynamic compromise). What is the most appropriate next management step regarding her endocrinology?

answers.text: Start oestrogen replacement immediately to induce puberty and improve quality of life

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oestrogen therapy is indicated to induce puberty in Turner syndrome, but it is typically deferred until the age of 12–13 years — after an adequate course of growth hormone — so as not to prematurely advance bone age and limit final height. Starting oestrogen at age 9 would close epiphyses too early.

answers.text: Begin recombinant growth hormone therapy to maximise adult height

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Growth hormone therapy is the first priority at this age. It significantly improves final adult height in Turner syndrome and should be started as early as the growth deficit is evident — often by 4–6 years or at diagnosis. Oestrogen replacement is introduced later (around 12–13 years) to avoid compromising final height. Cardiac surveillance for the bicuspid aortic valve should continue concurrently.

answers.text: Defer all hormonal treatment and observe until spontaneous puberty occurs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spontaneous puberty occurs in only ~10–20% of girls with Turner syndrome (those with partial X deletion or mosaicism). Waiting without treatment allows continued height loss and delayed puberty, both of which are preventable. Proactive treatment with GH (and later oestrogen) is the standard of care.

answers.text: Commence combined GH and oestrogen therapy simultaneously to address both height and puberty

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Simultaneous GH and oestrogen at age 9 risks accelerated bone maturation that limits final height. The standard approach is sequential: GH first (to maximise growth), then low-dose oestrogen from around 12–13 years to induce puberty in a physiological manner, increasing gradually over 2–3 years.

overallFeedback.feedback: Turner syndrome management is sequential: (1) growth hormone first — start when height deficit is clear, often well before puberty; (2) oestrogen replacement from ~12–13 years to induce puberty; (3) cardiac surveillance for associated lesions (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation). Starting oestrogen too early sacrifices final height.

Correct. In Turner syndrome, growth hormone therapy is started early (at age of growth concern, often pre-pubertally) to maximise final height. Oestrogen is deferred to ~12–13 years and introduced at low doses to mimic physiological puberty without prematurely closing epiphyses.
